Macro commodities ratio

Gold/Oil Ratio

This ratio shows how many barrels of WTI crude oil are equivalent to one ounce of gold. A rising ratio means gold is strengthening relative to oil; a falling ratio means oil is strengthening.

Loading Gold/Oil Ratio data…

Why macro investors watch this ratio

The Gold/Oil ratio is a classic macro indicator. When the ratio is high, gold is expensive relative to oil — often seen during periods of financial stress or low energy demand. When the ratio is low, oil is relatively expensive, often during periods of strong economic activity.

Some analysts use extreme readings of this ratio as contrarian signals for positioning in either commodity. It can also reflect relative inflation expectations between financial assets and energy markets.

Historical ranges and what they signal

The Gold/Oil ratio has historically ranged from around 6 to over 40 barrels per ounce of gold. During the 2008 financial crisis, oil prices collapsed from $147 per barrel, briefly sending the ratio above 25. In April 2020, when oil briefly traded at negative prices during the COVID-19 lockdown shock, the ratio hit an all-time extreme that is rarely shown on charts. Under normal market conditions, a ratio in the 15–25 range is considered historically average. Above 30 generally reflects energy market stress or gold being driven by safe-haven buying; below 15 reflects periods of strong global growth and tight energy markets.

In 2026, with gold trading near $3,200–$3,500 per ounce and WTI crude oil in the $70–$90 range, the ratio sits in the 35–45 range — elevated by historical standards, suggesting gold's monetary premium is running well ahead of energy market strength.

What drives each component of the ratio

Gold and oil are both denominated in US dollars, so a weaker dollar tends to push both prices higher and vice versa. But beyond that shared sensitivity, the two commodities respond to very different drivers. Gold is primarily driven by real interest rates, central bank reserve decisions, geopolitical stress and investor safe-haven demand. Industrial use accounts for only about 10% of gold consumption. Oil is driven by OPEC production decisions, global manufacturing activity, transportation demand, US inventory levels and the pace of the energy transition toward electric vehicles and renewables.

This means the Gold/Oil ratio can be read as a gauge of how much the financial economy (gold) is outpacing or lagging the real economy (oil). A persistently high ratio may signal that financial stress or monetary uncertainty is dominant; a low ratio may signal real economic activity and energy demand are running hot. Neither reading is precise, and both are better read in context with other macro indicators.

The energy transition and the ratio's long-run direction

One structural shift worth watching is the long-run impact of the energy transition on oil demand. As electric vehicles displace gasoline-powered cars and renewable energy captures a larger share of electricity generation, oil's long-run demand trajectory is under genuine pressure for the first time since the automobile era began. If oil demand peaks in the late 2020s or early 2030s, as some forecasters project, the Gold/Oil ratio may structurally drift higher over the long run — not because gold is more valuable, but because the floor under oil demand weakens. That said, near-term supply constraints from underinvestment in upstream exploration, combined with population and economic growth in emerging markets, could keep oil prices elevated for years before any structural decline materialises.
